# **Wind Energy Bird and Bat Monitoring Database Summary of the findings from post‐construction monitoring reports**

Environment Canada, the Canadian Wind Energy Association, Bird Studies Canada and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources

August 2012

## **INTRODUCTION**

This database is a joint initiative of Environment Canada, the Canadian Wind Energy Association, Bird Studies Canada and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources. The goals of this project are to facilitate improved understanding of the impacts of wind turbines on birds and bats, allow for greater consistency in assessment of wind power impacts across the country, and lead to future improvements in the Environmental Assessment and approval processes.

The database is intended to be a living tool that summarizes Canadian wind farm data collected and submitted to date, demonstrating our growth in understanding the effects of wind power on birds and bats, and evaluating survey methods and environmental effects assessment. The data summaries presented here represent our current state of knowledge based on Canadian data. This report is an updated version of the original database summary posted in November 2011. Since then, data from 17 studies has been incorporated into the database. The data summaries presented here represent a combination of data used in the original report and that provided in these newly available studies. These data expand the range of dates covered for 3 projects included in the original report and include 8 additional wind energy projects for which no data were previously available (see Table 1).

The current report presents uncorrected results from available studies, primarily conducted between 2006 and 2010. It represents the findings of approximately 239 months of postconstruction monitoring activity around 779 turbines at 24 different sites in Alberta, British Columbia, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan. Currently the database contains insufficient information to allow comparisons of species composition and seasonal fatality patterns between all provinces. However, to date, a significant amount of monitoring effort has been focused in Ontario, where 8077 of the 10526 (76%) turbine-months of monitoring included in the database have taken place. Therefore, this report presents data analysis on two spatial scales, the first includes information collected from all sites in Canada and the second only for those sites located in Ontario.

The database currently contains monitoring data from surveys conducted in all months of the year; however, the majority of mortality monitoring at wind installations occurred between the months of May and October. This reflects bird and bat monitoring protocols from provincial and federal regulators that recommend surveys be run from May 1[st] to October 31[st ] thus covering the main periods of activity of birds and bats, particularly during migration. Many wind installation projects did not undergo monitoring outside of these recommended periods and therefore the available information on mortality in this time frame is limited by the few sites that performed monitoring throughout the year.

## **METHODS**

## A. Species Composition:

Species composition of casualties can be used to identify which species have been the most frequently observed as casualties at Canadian wind farms. To draw patterns of species composition of casualties, we compared species ranks among sites. Within sites, species ranks are largely unaffected by the amount of effort devoted to monitoring. If a particular species was consistently found to be most prevalent in mortality reports at a majority of sites, this species would obtain the highest rank. This method allows a comparison between sites with different levels of monitoring effort, as each site is given an equal weight when calculating average ranks for each species.

It is important to realize that ranks within each site will be affected by other factors, such as the time of year when the monitoring occurred, or the type of turbines (height, capacity, blade area, etc.). It is hoped the database will provide the means to identify and understand casualty patterns linked to these other variables.

Ranks for birds and bats within each site were determined using fractional ranking, based on the total number of carcasses found for each species. With fractional ranking, items with equal numbers of carcasses receive the same ranking number, which corresponds to the minimum value of what they would have under ordinal rankings. In cases where the number of carcasses is zero for a given species within a project, we assigned the maximum rank possible across all sites. The total number of species reported across all sites was 9 for bats and 129 for birds. Therefore, all species that were not found at a given site were either given a fractional rank of 9 (for bats) and 129 (for birds). Without this correction, the rank assigned to species that had not been found at a specific site would be biased by the number of species found at that site.

## B. Seasonal Fatality Patterns:

To correct for the variation in survey effort throughout the year, seasonal fatality patterns are expressed as the number of carcasses found in each month divided by the number of wind turbines surveyed in that month (termed “turbine-months”). This allows for comparisons of the number of carcasses found between various months and seasons despite uneven sampling effort. It is important to note that the number of carcasses per turbine-month metric represents data that has not been corrected for confounding factors such as scavenger removal, searcher efficiency or percent area surveyed. It therefore does not represent the true level of mortality but, instead, serves as an index to facilitate a comparison of fatality rates seasonally. Some or all of the proposed correction factors have the potential to vary depending on the time of year, which may cause slight difference in the seasonal fatality patterns presented here.

## **RESULTS**

## A. Species Composition:

## 1. Bird and bat fatalities:

Across Canada, bat casualties were reported more often than birds at almost all sites monitored, accounting for 71% of all carcasses found (2270 bats and 945 birds). This pattern was consistent in Ontario, where 74% of the casualties found were bats (1928 bats; 674 birds).

## 2. Species composition: Birds (Canada)

Across Canada, a total of 945 bird casualties were found representing 129 different species. Passerines were most commonly found, representing 70% of all bird fatalities. The most prevalent species were: Horned Lark (11.69% of all bird carcasses found), Golden-crowned Kinglet (7.13% of all bird carcasses found) and European Starling (3.32% of all bird carcasses found). Raptors represented 7% of all birds found, with Turkey Vulture and Red-tailed Hawk found most commonly. Waterbirds, including waterfowl, represented 4% of all bird fatalities, with Mallard and Eared Grebe the most frequently reported waterbird species. ## 3. Species composition: Birds (Ontario)

Ontario bird fatality results were generally similar to the rest of Canada. In Ontario, 674 bird casualties were found representing 102 species. Passerines were most common, representing 67% of all bird fatalities in Ontario. The most prevalent passerine species were: Golden Crowned Kinglet (9.26% of all bird carcasses found), Red-eyed Vireo (6.52% of all bird carcasses found) and Horned Lark (3.09% of all bird carcasses found). Raptors represented 9% of all bird fatalities, with Turkey Vulture and Red-tailed Hawk found most commonly. Gulls represented 3% of all bird fatalities, with Ring-billed Gull the most often reported Gull species. Waterbirds represented 2% of all bird fatalities, with Canada Goose and Mallard the most frequently reported waterbird species. ## 4. Species composition: Bats (Canada)

Across Canada, a total of 2270 bat casualties were found representing 9 different species. Hoary Bat was the species most often found (33% of all bat fatalities). Silver-haired Bat was the second most commonly found species (23% of all bat fatalities). Other species commonly found included Big Brown Bat (8%), Little Brown Myotis (20%) and Eastern Red Bat (15%). Migratory bats (Eastern Red Bat, Hoary Bat and Silver-haired Bat) represented 71% of all bat mortalities. ## B. Seasonal Fatality Patterns

Seasonal fatality results in the following sections are reported as number of casualties (birds or bats) found per turbine, for each month. This summarizes the numbers of animals found during post construction monitoring surveys across all sites, and allows for comparison among months/across seasons. Estimated numbers of mortalities, which require correction for variation in sampling effort and scavenger take, could not be calculated from the data set.

- 6: Seasonal fatality patterns: Birds (Canada)

At wind farms in Canada, most of the bird carcasses were found from April through October. An examination of bird mortalities suggests a slight reduction in fatalities in June, possibly attributed to a decrease in bird movements outside of the migration season. 21% of all casualties were reported in April and May and 51% between the months of August and October. There were very few fatalities reported in winter and early spring (between November and March), a period when relatively few birds are present.

The overall pattern of fatalities was largely driven by passerines, which represented the majority of casualties. The fatality pattern for raptors and other non-waterbird species matched the pattern of passerines. No pattern was detected in waterbird fatalities across the year. The numbers of reported raptor and waterbird casualties were relatively low at most sites.

- 7: Seasonal patterns of fatalities: Birds (Ontario)

The seasonal pattern of bird fatalities was largely the same in Ontario, with highest fatalities reported between April and October. As with the Canadian results, increased fatalities were observed during migration periods in comparison to non-migratory seasons. Ontario fatality results are dominated by passerines, with relatively low numbers of raptors and waterfowl species reported across most sites.

- 8: Seasonal fatality patterns: Bats (Canada)

In Canada, most bat casualties at wind power projects were found in July, August and September (87% of bat carcasses) corresponding to the swarming and migratory period for bats. Peak numbers of carcasses were found in August (43% of all bat carcasses). Migratory (Hoary Bat, Silver-haired Bat, and Eastern Red Bat) species were found more than resident species (Little Brown Myotis Big Brown Bat, Eastern Pipistrelle, Northern Myotis and Eastern Small-footed Bat) in August and September.

The increase in fatalities of resident bat species between July and September coincides with the period of swarming behavior and movements between summer roosting sites and over winter hibernacula.

- 9: Seasonal patterns of fatalities: Bats (Ontario)

The seasonal pattern of reported bat fatalities at wind power projects in Ontario was largely the same as in the rest of Canada. In Ontario, most of the bat casualties were found in July, August and September (88% of all bat carcasses), with peak numbers occurring in August (45%).

Migratory (Hoary Bat, Silver-haired Bat, and Eastern Red Bat) and resident (Little Brown Myotis, Big Brown Bat, Eastern Pipistrelle, Northern Myotis and Eastern Small-footed Bat) species generally followed the same seasonal pattern. August was the month of highest reported carcasses for both migratory species (48% of all migratory bat casualties) and resident species (40% of all resident casualties).

## **CONCLUSIONS**

In general, the results and patterns of bird and bat fatalities, based on carcasses found per turbine-month, presented here are similar to those identified in the November 2011 summary report. Across Canada and within Ontario, the numbers of bat fatalities were higher than bird fatalities. Bird fatalities were dominated by passerines with relatively low numbers of raptors and waterbirds. The highest numbers of bird fatalities occur between April and October. Seasonal fatality patterns suggest a reduced number of bird fatalities in June, possibly linked to decreased migration activity during this period.

The highest numbers of bat fatalities occur between July and September (peaking in August) corresponding to the swarming and migratory period for bats. Migratory bat fatalities are slightly higher than resident bat fatalities and the seasonal distribution of fatalities follows a similar pattern for both guilds.

As data continues to be incorporated into the national wind energy bird and bat mortality monitoring database, opportunities to examine increasingly more in depth and detailed questions will emerge. Incorporating scavenger removal, searcher efficiency and percent area surveyed in future wind installation mortality surveys is a key area of focus. Templates for the collection of these data have been developed and are now publicly available.

_In memoriam_ : Matt Holder. The partners of the Wind Database project would like to acknowledge Matt Holder’s instrumental role in establishing the collaborative bird and bat monitoring database, and his contribution to this report. Before his untimely passing in 2011, Mr. Holder was an expert reviewer for wind energy research and impact assessment guidelines developed by Environment Canada, and was an expert contributor to similar initiatives at the provincial level. He served as a representative of the Canadian Wind Energy Association for numerous committees and initiatives, including a federal committee providing review of the Canadian Species at Risk Act. He was involved with over 100 wind power projects across Canada, and had a broad knowledge of wind energy development and associated environmental issues.
